name: Somalia
card_headline: Somalia's Supreme Court ruled the president's term extension unlawful, the government rejected it, and elections set for April and May 2027 lack opposition backing.
card_summary: The Supreme Court ruled on 5 November that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's one-year term extension is unlawful. His government rejected the ruling and replaced the chief justice. Parliamentary elections are set for 15 April 2027 and the presidential vote for 15 May. Talks with the opposition were scheduled for 14 to 18 November, and no outcome had been found by 25 November. Al-Shabaab holds much of the countryside, Uganda began withdrawing troops on 29 October, and about 6 million people face crisis-level hunger.
card_local: Garowe Online reported that parliament's mandate expired on 14 April and that the speaker extended it by a year. Shabelle Media reported on 12 November that former president Farmaajo's party denied joining a joint meeting with the government. [1][2]
card_international: AFP reports that the Supreme Court ruled the extension unlawful on 5 November and that Mohamud had moved to dismiss the chief justice. Al Jazeera reports that the electoral commission is keeping the April and May 2027 dates. [3][4]
card_scholar: Crisis Group, as summarised by Dawan Africa, finds that the African Union mission has fallen from about 22,000 to roughly 12,000 troops and expects gradual erosion of government control rather than a sudden collapse. The Critical Threats Project assesses that al-Shabaab may exploit the political crisis near Mogadishu. [5][6]
context_md: Somaliland declared independence in 1991 and is not recognised by most states, though Israel recognised it in December 2025. [4][7] Hassan Sheikh Mohamud took power in 2022. [8] The system has been indirect: clan leaders select electoral colleges for the 275 parliamentary seats, and parliament then elects the president. [9] Parliament passed the first constitutional amendments in 2024 and the rest in March 2026, which lengthened presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years. [4] Mogadishu held direct elections for 390 district council posts on 25 December 2025. [9] Al-Shabaab retook most of Hiraan and Middle Shabelle in an early 2025 counteroffensive. [10] The government recognised Northeastern State as its sixth federal member state in January 2026, and Somaliland still claims that territory. [11]

sections.title: The Supreme Court says the term extension is unlawful, and the government has replaced the chief justice
sections.body_md:
Mohamud took power in 2022, and AFP reports that he argues an amended constitution passed by parliament this year gave him an extra year. [8] Parliament's own four-year mandate expired on 14 April, when Speaker Adan Madobe said parliament would stay a year to support a move to one-person, one-vote elections and several MPs resigned in protest. [1] The government declared a "transition period" in May, despite an earlier agreement with the opposition on holding elections. [8]

On 5 November the Supreme Court ruled the extension unlawful. It held that the amendments did not apply to his current term and that he should have left office in May. [3] Al Jazeera says five judges ruled the extensions could not apply to officials already in office, and that the presidency had removed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed the day before. [4] The court called the dismissal "null and void", and AFP carried unconfirmed reports that Ahmed was under arrest. [3] The Critical Threats Project reports that the court ordered an election plan within 30 days and federal elections within 90 days, that the opposition Somali Future Council endorsed the ruling, and that the government rejected it and installed a replacement that the Council denounced. [6]

The electoral commission announced on 15 October that parliamentary elections would be held on 15 April 2027 and the presidential vote on 15 May. [8] The Standard says the electoral body set these dates unilaterally and that the core dispute is one-person, one-vote against the indirect clan-based delegate system. [12] Al Jazeera describes the plan as direct election of lower-house members by citizens, with parliament still choosing the president. [4] The Africa Center adds that the voter registry is outdated and that some fear direct voting could favour Mohamud's supporters in safer urban areas. [9]

Talks were scheduled for 14 to 18 November. The Critical Threats Project says the United States, Turkey, the United Kingdom and the European Union were reportedly involved and that the government signalled openness to technical compromises while still planning direct elections. [6] The Standard names no third-party mediator and says nothing concrete has come from meetings since February. [12] Farmaajo's party said he received the armed forces commanders at his home, that they carried a message from the president, and that talks should resume from where they broke down on 3 September. [2] This draft found no report of how the November talks ended.

lenses.local: Garowe Online reported lawmakers resigning on 14 April, one of them refusing to hold a seat through an extension without broad consensus. [1]
lenses.international: AFP and Al Jazeera report the ruling and the chief justice's removal, and Al Jazeera adds that the commission has kept its April and May 2027 dates. [3][4]
lenses.scholar: The Critical Threats Project describes a government open to technical compromise but committed to direct elections, and the Chatham House podcast of 12 June says the amendments created a political impasse. [6][13]

sections.title: Puntland and Jubaland have pulled back, and armed revolts have opened in South West and Hirshabelle
sections.body_md:
Puntland and Jubaland both rejected the 2024 amendments, according to Al Jazeera. Puntland withdrew cooperation with the federal government, and Jubaland followed after a dispute over electoral legislation. Both have their own security forces and revenue and argue that agreements made without them cannot bind them. Puntland's president, Said Abdullahi Deni, suggested Somalis may need to reconsider how the country holds together. [4] Clashes between federal and Jubaland forces in December 2024 killed dozens. [9]

In South West State the federal government rejected the disputed indirect re-election of Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen in March. Federal troops took Baidoa on 30 March, and AP says he announced his resignation. [14] The Critical Threats Project calls him deposed and says forces loyal to him have captured three district capitals and attacked Baidoa at least nine times, most recently on 2 November. [6] After fighting in Baidoa on 17 August, a hospital emergency head told AP that at least 4 civilians were killed and 98 wounded. The federal government said nearly 30 attackers died and South West authorities said about 50. Neither toll was verified. The federal government says the attackers included al-Shabaab fighters. [14] The Critical Threats Project assesses that the opposition forces are almost certainly deconflicting with al-Shabaab and possibly coordinating with it. [6]

In Hirshabelle the Hawadle clan rebelled in late October over the federal choice of a state president from another clan. Hawadle militiamen seized government facilities in Beledweyne on 30 October, and the rebel leader, Abdullahi Sanbalolshe, rejected an 8 November offer to move the state capital to Hiiraan. Al-Shabaab announced a peace agreement with Hawadle factions in early October. [6]

In Somaliland, which Israel recognised in December 2025, authorities reportedly arrested a would-be candidate for Somalia's presidency and the journalist who interviewed him, as covered in the rights section below. [7]

lenses.local: Local sourcing on the state revolts is thin in this draft.
lenses.international: AP carried the August Baidoa fighting with its competing death tolls, and Al Jazeera carried the positions of Puntland and Jubaland. [14][4]
lenses.scholar: The Critical Threats Project tracks the South West and Hirshabelle revolts and the possible link to al-Shabaab. [6]

sections.title: Al-Shabaab: a managed stalemate that may tilt as foreign support shrinks
sections.body_md:
The Somali Guardian, citing a Crisis Group report released that week, describes a stalemate. Federal forces and clan militias took large areas of Hiraan and Middle Shabelle in 2022 and 2023 but could not hold them. Al-Shabaab retook most of both in early 2025. Its push into Lower Shabelle met stronger resistance from Somali forces, African Union troops and air power, with US and Turkish help, and by the second half of 2025 both sides had consolidated. [10] Somalia's Ministry of Defence rejected the Crisis Group report, saying it contained factual inaccuracies and wrongly portrayed al-Shabaab as more restrained toward civilians. The report itself was not located for this draft. [15]

AFP reports that al-Shabaab controls much of the country and that heavy gunfire between rival political factions hit Mogadishu in June. [8] The Critical Threats Project says al-Shabaab attacks in South West have risen by roughly 35 percent since March and that it has repeatedly assessed that the group may exploit the political crisis to target sensitive areas in and around Mogadishu. [6] A UN expert panel told the Security Council in December 2025 that al-Shabaab is the greatest threat to peace in Somalia and the region, and put ISIS-Somalia at over 1,000 fighters at the end of 2024, at least 60 percent of them foreign. [16]

AFRICOM told New America that it had conducted 63 strikes in Somalia in 2026 as of 29 May, with 26 in January, 16 in February, 7 in March, 12 in April and 2 in May. The last declared strike in that tally was on 6 May and targeted ISIS-Somalia near the Golis Mountains. AFRICOM denied a disputed 22 April strike. [17] The Critical Threats Project says US forces left Baledogle Air Base in late October. [6]

lenses.local: The Somali Guardian and Shabelle Media carry both the Crisis Group assessment and the defence ministry's rejection of it. [10][15]
lenses.international: AFP reports that al-Shabaab controls much of the country and that little election progress has been made beyond a few local pockets. [8]
lenses.scholar: New America counts AFRICOM's declared strikes, and the Critical Threats Project tracks al-Shabaab's use of the political crisis. [17][6]

sections.title: The African Union mission has shrunk to about 12,000 troops, and its UN support is renewed for one year only
sections.body_md:
Crisis Group's report of 18 September, as summarised by Dawan Africa, says the African Union mission (AUSSOM) has fallen from about 22,000 troops to roughly 12,000 as donor support declined. It finds weaknesses in every replacement option, expects bilateral arrangements with Uganda, Kenya, Ethiopia, Turkey and the United States, and thinks gradual erosion of government control is likelier than sudden collapse. It warns that a replacement system may need to be working by the second half of 2027. [5]

The Daily Monitor reports that the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) cut its funding by 25 percent and was due to end logistical support on 31 December 2026, after the US told the African Union in July it would not back renewal of the mandate at the Security Council in December. It also reports that Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announced on X on 29 October that Uganda had started withdrawing its troops. [18] The Critical Threats Project dates the start of the withdrawal of Uganda's roughly 2,000 troops to 2 November and says all AUSSOM contributors plan to leave by the end of 2027. [6]

On 17 November Kenyans.co.ke reported that the US would support a one-year renewal of the UNSOS and AUSSOM mandates, and that Somalia's government welcomed the decision in a statement dated 16 November. The article gives no amount or conditions, and says the administration had argued in July that Somalia had not made enough progress against al-Shabaab. [19] The Africa Center's undated page says roughly 11,000 troops from neighbouring countries serve in AUSSOM and that Egypt has committed up to 10,000 more. [9]

lenses.local: Local sourcing on the mission's funding is thin in this draft.
lenses.international: The Daily Monitor and Kenyans.co.ke report the Ugandan exit and the US reversal on UN support. [18][19]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group argues that delay is the main danger and that Somali units must be prepared to take over vacated positions. [5]

sections.title: About 6 million people face crisis-level hunger, and the 2026 appeal is 30 percent funded
sections.body_md:
A joint UN release of 15 May said about 6 million people, or 31 percent of the population, faced IPC phase 3 or worse between April and June 2026. Close to 1.9 million were in phase 4 (emergency), a number that had tripled in less than a year. About 1.9 million children were acutely malnourished, including 493,000 with severe acute malnutrition. The release flagged famine risk among agropastoral populations in Burhakaba district, Bay region, where nearly 40 percent of children under five were acutely malnourished. [20]

The Norwegian Refugee Council wrote on 27 August that more than 700,000 people had been displaced this year, over 500,000 of them by drought. It said donors had provided 30 percent of the money needed for the 2026 response, citing OCHA, and warned that the coming Deyr rains could bring the worst flooding since 2023, which displaced 1.2 million people. [21] OCHA's plan, launched on 26 January, asks for US$852 million to help 2.4 million people. It counts 4.8 million people in need, a 20 percent fall from 2025 that OCHA's own text attributes to stricter criteria and not to better conditions. [22]

Human Rights Watch reported that authorities carried out forced evictions in Mogadishu in 2025, including of displaced people in camps. [23] An opinion piece in Addis Standard by Somali researcher Abdinasir Ali Osman cites UNICEF as saying 205 health and nutrition facilities had closed by 21 August, and says the figures are agency estimates that should not be added together. [24]

lenses.local: Local sourcing on hunger is thin in this draft.
lenses.international: UNICEF, NRC and OCHA are the main sources on the hunger figures, displacement and funding. [20][21][22]
lenses.scholar: Abdinasir Ali Osman argues in Addis Standard that aid keeps services running but that bypassing state systems limits lasting capacity. [24]

sections.title: Growth is near 3 percent, aid is falling, and diaspora money is the buffer
sections.body_md:
The World Bank said on 13 May that real growth slowed to about 3 percent in 2025 from about 4 percent in 2023 and 2024, and projected 2.8 percent in 2026 and 3.1 percent in 2027. Consumer prices rose 3.7 percent in 2025 and are projected to rise 6 percent in 2026. It names reduced humanitarian and security assistance as a main driver of the slowdown. [25] The IMF's staff statement of 5 October is lower: 2.3 percent growth in 2026, 2.7 percent in 2027 and inflation of 6.5 percent in 2026. It rates risks as high, including more severe climate shocks, regional conflict and further aid cuts, and calls the external position vulnerable though remittances are resilient. [26] The two institutions' forecasts for 2026 differ by 0.5 percentage points. [25][26]

The East African, citing the Central Bank of Somalia, reports that remittances rose 5 percent to a record $6.78 billion in 2025 from $6.43 billion in 2024. [27] The World Bank adds that 71 percent of households have electricity access but only 21 percent get more than eight hours a day, and that generation is almost entirely diesel. [25] The state has little revenue of its own: the Addis Standard opinion piece cites World Bank data for 2022 showing federal domestic revenue of about $262 million, or 2.2 percent of GDP, and an IMF estimate that aid may have been 20 to 30 percent of GDP over the previous decade. [24] The IMF mission also mentions a planned petroleum licensing round. [26]

lenses.local: Local sourcing on the economy is thin in this draft; The East African is a Nairobi outlet. [27]
lenses.international: The World Bank and IMF agree on slow growth and rising inflation and differ on the size of the slowdown. [25][26]
lenses.scholar: Abdinasir Ali Osman argues that weak domestic revenue and off-budget aid keep the state dependent on donors. [24]

sections.title: Journalists are detained in Las Anod and Hargeisa, and a 2025 ban on reporting security threats was announced
sections.body_md:
Human Rights Watch's World Report 2026, covering 2025, says the information minister announced in March a ban on reporting on issues that could pose a "security threat". After the 18 March bombing of the presidential convoy, police briefly detained at least 22 journalists and media workers and shut down an outlet. In September four TikTokers and another person were reportedly arrested over a dance video allegedly insulting the president. HRW also reports that military courts continued to hand down death sentences in terrorism cases. [23]

CPJ says journalist Abdiqani Abdirahman Mohamed, known as Dhulmar, was arrested in Las Anod on 26 March 2026 and held without charge. A Las Anod court remanded him for seven days on 27 March. His arrest followed an interview with a former presidential adviser, Abdirisak Mohamed Warsame, who criticised the president and said regional forces were unpaid. Police said the case against Abdirisak concerned fake news and libel of security forces, and officials did not answer CPJ. [11]

In Somaliland, CPJ says Abdirahman Mohamed Ege of Horn Cable TV has been held without charge in Hargeisa since 22 October after interviewing Abdiqadir Sharay, who plans to run for president of Somalia in 2027 and was reportedly arrested on 16 October. CPJ says Somaliland authorities have made numerous arrests of journalists over the past year, and that another journalist, Abdiqani Hussein Abokor, has been held since 29 August. Somaliland's information ministry and presidency did not respond to CPJ. [7]

lenses.local: Local sourcing on press freedom is thin in this draft; the Somali Journalists Syndicate and a defence lawyer supplied details of the Las Anod arrest to CPJ. [11]
lenses.international: HRW and CPJ are the main sources on arrests, the reporting ban and military-court sentences. [23][11][7]
lenses.scholar: No academic research on press freedom in Somalia was reviewed for this draft.

timeline.text: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud takes power as president.
In an early-2025 counteroffensive, al-Shabaab retakes most of Hiraan and Middle Shabelle.
Israel recognises Somaliland; a UN expert panel names al-Shabaab the greatest threat to peace in the region.
Mogadishu holds direct elections for 390 district council posts.
The government recognises Northeastern State as its sixth federal member state.
Federal troops take Baidoa from forces loyal to South West leader Laftagareen.
Parliament's four-year mandate expires; the speaker extends it by one year and several MPs resign.
The government declares a transition period as the presidential mandate ends without an election deal.
Fighting in Baidoa kills at least 4 civilians and wounds 98, according to a hospital head.
Crisis Group publishes a report on Somalia's security order as the AU mission drawdown looms.
The electoral commission sets parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and the presidential vote for 15 May.
Uganda's Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces that withdrawal of Ugandan troops has started.
Hawadle militiamen seize government facilities in Beledweyne.
The Supreme Court rules the term extension unlawful; the presidency had moved to dismiss the chief justice the day before.
Talks between the government and opposition are scheduled to open, running to 18 November; no outcome was found.
The US announces support for a one-year renewal of the UNSOS and AUSSOM mandates.

factchecks.claim: President Mohamud's term was lawfully extended by one year.
factchecks.by: The federal government and parliament's leadership, 2026
factchecks.evidence: The Supreme Court ruled on 5 November that the extension was unlawful and that he should have left office in May. The government rejected the ruling and moved to dismiss the chief justice, and the court called that dismissal null and void. Parliament's speaker had said in April that the extension supports a move to one-person, one-vote elections, and the government says it prevents a power vacuum.

factchecks.claim: Somalia's next president will be chosen by direct popular vote.
factchecks.by: Government plans for one-person, one-vote elections, as reported in 2026
factchecks.evidence: Al Jazeera reports that citizens would directly elect lower-house members while parliament still elects the president. The Standard describes the core dispute as one-person, one-vote against the indirect clan-based system, and the Critical Threats Project says the government still plans direct elections. A direct vote for members of parliament is planned, but the sources read for this draft do not describe a direct presidential vote. A Standard headline seen in search results suggests a direct presidential vote in May, but that page could not be opened.

scores.coverage_basis: AFP and AP file on Somalia mostly when something breaks, such as the Supreme Court ruling or the Baidoa fighting [3][14]. Think tanks publish steadily, with Critical Threats Project, Crisis Group and New America material in the past year [6][17][5], and Garowe Online and Shabelle Media cover the political story in detail [1][2].

severity.basis: AFRICOM declared 63 strikes in 2026 to 29 May, Baidoa fighting in August left at least 4 civilians dead and 98 wounded, and al-Shabaab controls much of the countryside [17][14][8].
About 6 million people are in IPC phase 3 or worse, close to 1.9 million in phase 4, with famine risk in Burhakaba, and the 2026 response was 30 percent funded by August [20][21].
The government moved to replace the chief justice after the Supreme Court ruling, and CPJ documents detentions of journalists in Las Anod and Hargeisa [4][11][7].
Growth is projected at 2.3 to 2.8 percent in 2026 with inflation at 6 to 6.5 percent, and the IMF rates risks as high [25][26].
The mandate dispute, armed revolts in South West and Hirshabelle, a 25 percent UNSOS cut and the Ugandan exit all arrived within about seven months, and famine risk has emerged [6][18][20].

parts.basis: The US declared 63 strikes in 2026 to 29 May and left Baledogle in late October, Egypt has committed up to 10,000 troops, and US and Turkish help stopped al-Shabaab's push on Lower Shabelle [17][6][9][10].
The Africa Center says Houthi and pirate attacks threaten shipping in the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea off Somalia's coast, while Somalia's own economy grows about 3 percent a year [9][25].
Crisis Group expects bilateral security deals with Uganda, Kenya, Ethiopia, Turkey and the US to fill the gap left by AUSSOM, and the Africa Center says ISIS keeps a base in Puntland [5][9].
Remittances reached a reported $6.78 billion in 2025 and more than 700,000 people were displaced in 2026 by late August [27][21].
Israel recognised Somaliland in December 2025, and the UN logistics model for the AU mission was due to end on 31 December 2026 before the US renewal [4][18][19].

summary: Somalia matters beyond its borders through the fight against al-Shabaab, the future of the AU mission and the competition among foreign backers, more than through trade [5][6].
gi.up: A sustained al-Shabaab advance on Mogadishu, or an end to the AU mission without a replacement.
gi.down: A negotiated election deal and a funded transition plan for Somali forces.

gaps: The outcome of the 14 to 18 November talks was not found; the latest political source is Al Jazeera on 19 November.
Crisis Group's own reports of 30 June and 18 September were not opened; they are read through the Somali Guardian, Shabelle Media and Dawan Africa summaries.
The electoral commission's own statement was not located; the election dates rest on AFP and Al Jazeera.

Dates conflict between sources: the chief justice's removal is 4 November in AFP and Al Jazeera but 7 November in the Critical Threats Project, and Uganda's withdrawal is announced on 29 October (Daily Monitor) but begins on 2 November (Critical Threats Project).
Local sourcing is thin: only Garowe Online, the Somali Guardian and Shabelle Media were read, one or two articles each. Hiiraan, Caasimada, Horseed and Somali-language outlets were not read.
AFRICOM strike counts stop at 29 May 2026; later strikes, including a search result about a November strike near Jamaame, were not opened.
No ACLED or UN count of 2026 civilian casualties from al-Shabaab attacks was retrieved.
The Africa Center page has no date and its facts may be out of date; troop figures for AUSSOM differ (about 11,000 there, roughly 12,000 from Crisis Group).
Remittance figures rest on one article that gives no date; the Central Bank's annual report was not opened.
The IPC figures are for April to June 2026; no later Deyr-season update or flood outcome was found.
The roles of Turkey, Egypt, the UAE and Ethiopia, and Israel's recognition of Somaliland, are covered only briefly.
No peer-reviewed academic research on Somalia from the past 12 months was reviewed.

scholar_md:
The Critical Threats Project describes a government open to technical compromise but committed to direct elections, and the Chatham House podcast of 12 June says the amendments created a political impasse. [6][13]
